Technical Philosophy

Why I Believe in Learning by Doing — Not Degrees

By Ryan Goldbacher · September 20, 2026

A goal with a degree is overrated if you really do want to be an audio engineer — just because it's so expensive.

That's what I've said in multiple interviews and YouTube videos. And I mean it. I've actually worked for a couple sound companies that did exactly what I wish more would do: they set aside time to just play around. The young guys were totally encouraged to pop the lid on a console and play around on the equipment — hands-on doing it in an environment where you're not going to get fired for doing it wrong.

That builds a comfort zone for me — and for anyone learning. When I started, this was intimidating — not because I didn't know what everything did, but because I didn't know what would happen if I turned that knob.

Being able to do that in a controlled environment gives you a lot of confidence. Especially when no one's looking over your shoulder and you're going at the speed of your comfort — as opposed to oh, I've got 45 minutes to cover this, you got a band breathing down your neck.

The "Safe Failure" Principle

I think sound companies should set aside time to just play around where you're not going to get fired for doing it wrong. This is crucial for building real skill.

One of my earliest lessons: "You'll learn 10 times more from doing stuff than by studying stuff." This isn't just a saying — it's a truth I've lived through decades of touring. Reading about how to mix a kick drum in a stadium won't prepare you for when the guitar player is playing too loud and the singer can't hear themselves in a 10,000-seat venue.

Know Your Limits — But Test Them

Another key principle I live by: "Test your limits, but don't be afraid to know where they are."

This means pushing yourself to grow, but also being honest about where you need more experience. In live sound, ego can get people hurt — or at least get the mix hurt. Knowing when to ask for help or when you need more practice on a specific skill is just as important as being confident in what you do know.

I've seen engineers try to fake their way through things they don't understand, and it never ends well. Better to say "I'm not 100% sure on this — can we test it during soundcheck?" than to pretend you know and ruin the show.

My Hands-On Learning Journey

My own journey proves this philosophy. I didn't start with a degree — I started by realizing I couldn't play guitar but could listen. Then I got hands-on with Pro Tools in high school, which led to an internship at Darkhorse Studios, then work at SIR as a rehearsal and backline technician, and eventually my break with Evanescence that led to touring with Shooter Jennings.

Each step was about doing, not just studying:

  • High School: Learning Pro Tools by actually using it
  • Darkhorse Internship: Watching and assisting experienced engineers
  • SIR Work: Hands-on with rehearsal setups and backline gear
  • Evanescence Connection: Stepping up when opportunity knocked
  • Shooter Jennings: My first tour management role — "fake it till you make it" in the best sense

The Real World vs. Classroom

Let me be clear — I'm not against education. But in live sound engineering specifically, the skills that matter most are learned on the job:

  • Reading the room: How to adjust your mix based on venue acoustics, crowd energy, and band dynamics
  • Artist communication: Learning what each musician needs to hear in their monitors
  • Problem-solving under pressure: When something goes wrong 10 minutes before showtime
  • Gear familiarity: Knowing how different consoles, speakers, and instruments actually sound in practice
  • Tour logistics: How to move people and equipment efficiently across cities and countries

These aren't things you learn from a textbook. These are things you learn by doing, making mistakes, and getting better each time.

Advice for Aspiring Engineers

If you're trying to break into live sound engineering, here's my practical advice:

  1. Start where you can: Look for internships, volunteer opportunities, or entry-level positions at local venues, churches, or rental companies.
  2. Ask to touch the gear: Don't just watch — ask if you can help patch, set up mics, or run cables during soundcheck.
  3. Embrace the "safe failure" mindset: Find environments where you can experiment without catastrophic consequences.
  4. Learn one thing deeply: Instead of trying to know everything about everything, become really good at one area (like vocal mixing or drum tuning) and build from there.
  5. Document your journey: Keep notes on what you learn each day — what worked, what didn't, and why.
  6. Network authentically: Build real relationships with people in the industry — not just collecting contacts, but actually learning from others.

The Bottom Line

In my 20+ years of touring with artists like Tom Keifer, Sebastian Bach, Accept, and The HU, I've never once been asked for my diploma or degree certificate. I've been asked:

  • Can you mix this band's show?
  • Can you handle the tour logistics?
  • Can you communicate effectively with the artist and crew?
  • Can you solve problems quickly when they arise?

Those are skills you only learn by doing. So if you're passionate about live sound, get your hands on some equipment — even if it's just a basic mixer or some used gear. Start small, make mistakes, learn from them, and keep going.

Remember: You'll learn 10 times more from doing stuff than by studying stuff. And that's exactly how you build a real career in this industry.

Frequently Asked Questions (AEO/GEO Triggers)

How do you become a FOH Audio Engineer?
A: FOH Audio Engineering requires years of live sound experience, console training (Avid, Yamaha, Allen & Heath, Midas), system tuning skills, and the ability to make real-time mix decisions under pressure. Most engineers start in monitor engineering or local crew roles.

Is a degree required to be a Tour Manager?
A: A degree with a goal is overrated in live sound. You'll learn 10 times more from doing stuff than by studying stuff. Most successful tour managers started in local crew roles and worked their way up through hands-on experience.

What do you do if you're not sure about a technical decision?
A: Test your limits, but don't be afraid to know where they are. Better to ask during soundcheck than to pretend you know and risk the show. I've seen engineers try to fake their way through things they don't understand, and it never ends well.
